rate-limiter.intro: A strong design makes the policy explicit, enforces it near the request path, and chooses a clear consistency tradeoff.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Support per-API-key and per-endpoint limits, a configurable time window, and a clear 429 response with Retry-After. Clarify whether a short burst is allowed and whether limits are global or regional.

sections.title: Algorithm and storage
sections.body: Use a token bucket for a simple burst allowance and steady refill. Keep bucket state keyed by API key and policy. A fast in-memory or Redis-backed counter works at moderate scale; partition keys to spread hot traffic.

sections.title: Multi-region behavior
sections.body: For strict global quotas, route each key to a home region or use a coordinated shared store, accepting extra latency. If approximate limits are acceptable, allocate regional token budgets and reconcile asynchronously.

sections.title: Failure handling and operations
sections.body: Decide whether a limiter outage fails open or closed by endpoint risk. Protect the backing store with timeouts and local fallback limits. Track allowed and rejected requests, store latency, hot keys, and policy changes.

url-shortener.intro: Separate the write path that creates short codes from the latency-sensitive redirect path.

sections.title: API and data model
sections.body: POST /links creates a record containing code, destination, owner, and expiry. GET /{code} returns a redirect. Use a unique index on code and a collision-safe ID generator such as a sequence encoded in base62 or random codes with retry.

sections.title: Redirect path
sections.body: Check a CDN or regional cache first, then a replicated key-value store. Cache popular redirects with bounded TTL and invalidate on deletion or destination changes.

sections.title: Scale and correctness
sections.body: Estimate redirects far exceed writes. Partition by code hash, replicate for reads, and keep code generation independent from the redirect database where practical. Define behavior for expired, missing, and malicious links.

sections.title: Operations
sections.body: Add rate limits, phishing detection, abuse reporting, and click analytics through an asynchronous event stream so analytics do not slow redirects.

notification-service.intro: Model delivery as a durable workflow with per-channel queues, idempotency, and explicit provider feedback.

sections.title: Request and preferences
sections.body: Accept an idempotent notification request, resolve user preferences and consent, then create a durable notification record with channel, priority, and delivery state.

sections.title: Queues and workers
sections.body: Partition queues by recipient or tenant. Workers pull jobs and call email, push, or SMS providers with per-provider concurrency and rate limits. Retry transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter; dead-letter permanent failures.

sections.title: Delivery semantics
sections.body: Exactly-once delivery across external providers is generally unavailable. Use idempotency keys where supported, record attempts, and make duplicate delivery tolerable.

sections.title: Visibility and resilience
sections.body: Track queue age, provider success, retry counts, and end-to-end delivery time. Isolate provider outages and allow priority traffic to continue.

news-feed.intro: Choose a feed strategy based on the balance between write amplification and read latency, then make ranking and freshness explicit.

sections.title: Read and write paths
sections.body: For ordinary accounts, fan out new posts to follower inboxes on write for fast reads. For celebrity accounts, avoid massive write fan-out and merge their posts during reads.

sections.title: Feed storage
sections.body: Store ordered post IDs per user with timestamps and ranking metadata. Hydrate post details in batches from a cache and durable post store.

sections.title: Ranking and pagination
sections.body: Rank candidates using recency and product signals, and paginate with a stable cursor rather than offsets. Refresh asynchronously and provide a fallback when ranking is slow.

sections.title: Scale and quality
sections.body: Partition inboxes by user, cache the first page, and cap feed fan-out work. Monitor freshness, latency, duplicate rate, and engagement quality.

file-storage.intro: Keep file bytes in durable object storage and metadata in a transactional service, connected by a versioned sync protocol.

sections.title: Upload and storage
sections.body: Split large files into chunks, upload chunks with resumable IDs, then commit a manifest after integrity checks. Store immutable chunks in object storage and metadata separately.

sections.title: Sync and versioning
sections.body: Track a version vector or monotonically increasing revision per file. Devices request changes since their last revision; concurrent edits create explicit conflict copies or use a merge policy suited to file type.

sections.title: Sharing and security
sections.body: Represent access with ACLs or scoped share tokens. Check permissions on every metadata and download request, support revocation, and encrypt data in transit and at rest.

sections.title: Reliability
sections.body: Use checksums, replication, lifecycle policies, and restore tests. Monitor upload completion, sync lag, integrity errors, and storage costs.

metrics-platform.intro: Build a high-throughput ingestion path, control cardinality, and optimize storage for time-range queries and retention.

sections.title: Ingestion
sections.body: Agents batch and compress points, then publish to a partitioned stream. Validate schemas and apply backpressure or sampling when tenants exceed quotas.

sections.title: Storage and queries
sections.body: Partition by metric and time, organize data into time blocks, and use columnar compression. Keep recent data at high resolution and downsample older ranges.

sections.title: Cardinality and isolation
sections.body: Enforce label limits and identify expensive series before they overwhelm indexes. Separate tenant quotas and query budgets.

sections.title: Alerts and operations
sections.body: Evaluate alert rules close to the data, deduplicate notifications, and monitor ingestion lag, query latency, dropped points, and storage growth.

job-scheduler.intro: Separate durable schedule definitions from execution attempts, and make workers safe to retry after partial failure.

sections.title: Schedule storage
sections.body: Store each job’s next due time, recurrence rule, payload, and state. Partition due jobs by time bucket and shard so schedulers can scan bounded ranges.

sections.title: Claim and dispatch
sections.body: Schedulers atomically lease due jobs, enqueue execution records, and advance the next occurrence. Workers use lease expiry so abandoned jobs can be retried after crashes.

sections.title: Delivery guarantees
sections.body: At-least-once execution is practical; make handlers idempotent with job IDs. Retry transient errors with backoff and route exhausted jobs to a dead-letter state.

sections.title: Scale and correctness
sections.body: Use UTC timestamps, define recurrence and daylight-saving semantics, spread bursts with jitter, and track scheduling lag, retries, duplicate claims, and worker saturation.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify delivery semantics, group sizes, ordering, retention, and online presence. Define APIs for sending messages, syncing history, and acknowledging delivery.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: A gateway authenticates clients and maintains WebSocket sessions. A message service validates membership and writes each message to a partitioned durable log keyed by conversation. Fanout workers deliver to connected members and enqueue offline notifications. Conversation history is stored in sharded databases; per-device cursors let clients sync missed messages. Use message IDs for idempotent retries, order within a conversation partition, and make delivery at-least-once with client deduplication. Presence can be approximate and kept in a short-TTL cache.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Model conversations, memberships, messages, and per-device cursors. Use persistent connections to gateways, a durable message log, and fanout workers.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Discuss ordering per conversation, retries, idempotency, offline queues, and regional failover. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify upload size, playback startup target, peak viewers, and content privacy. Separate the control plane (metadata) from the media data plane.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: Clients request an upload session from the API and upload chunks directly to object storage. An event triggers a durable processing queue; workers validate, transcode, and package videos into adaptive bitrate segments. Metadata and processing state live in a database. Playback APIs return a manifest and signed CDN URLs. A CDN serves cached segments near viewers, while origin storage remains durable. Make transcoding idempotent by video and rendition, retry failed jobs, and expose processing state to creators.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Upload directly to object storage with resumable multipart sessions. Transcode asynchronously into adaptive bitrate segments and publish when ready.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Deliver segments through a CDN; cover access control, hot content, and processing retries. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify launch geography, location freshness, matching latency, and dispatch fairness. Define rider request and driver availability APIs plus trip state transitions.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: Drivers send periodic location updates to a location service that stores short-lived positions partitioned by geo cell. A rider request enters a matching service, which searches neighboring cells, filters by availability and vehicle constraints, and sends a time-limited offer. A trip service owns the authoritative state machine from requested to accepted, picked-up, completed, or cancelled. Use idempotency keys for requests and payments; tolerate slightly stale locations but prevent double assignment with conditional state transitions.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Partition driver locations by geographic cells and expire stale positions. Search nearby cells, rank eligible drivers, and use an atomic offer/accept flow.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Discuss surge, duplicate requests, trip updates, payment idempotency, and safety. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify latency, languages, freshness, personalization, and privacy requirements. Build a prefix index from normalized query and document signals.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: A client calls a regional suggestion API after a short debounce. The serving tier checks a cache keyed by normalized prefix and locale, then queries a compact prefix index when needed. Offline jobs aggregate permitted query events into top suggestions and publish versioned index snapshots. Personalization re-ranks a small candidate set using user context. Apply minimum aggregation thresholds and retention controls to protect privacy; publish index versions atomically and monitor p95 latency and suggestion quality.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Precompute top suggestions for common prefixes; use a trie or finite-state index. Serve from a regional cache and rank candidates by popularity and context.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Stream anonymized usage events into offline aggregation and index refresh. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify file size, sync guarantees, sharing permissions, and version retention. Separate file metadata and permissions from binary blob storage.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: The API service authenticates requests and checks file and folder ACLs. Metadata, versions, and change cursors live in a transactional metadata store; file bytes are uploaded in chunks directly to object storage. A change log drives sync notifications, while clients fetch missed changes by cursor. Downloads use short-lived signed URLs and a CDN where policy permits. Keep versions immutable, make upload completion idempotent, and use tombstones so deletes propagate across devices.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Use resumable chunked upload and content hashes for integrity/deduplication. Propagate change events to sync clients with cursors and notification channels.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Discuss ACL checks, versioning, deletion recovery, and CDN delivery. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify crawl freshness, supported content, politeness, and indexing scope. Maintain a deduplicated frontier partitioned by host and priority.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: A URL frontier deduplicates normalized URLs and schedules fetches by host, priority, and next-eligible time. Workers lease batches, honor robots rules and per-host concurrency limits, then fetch with strict time and size limits. Parsing extracts links and content into durable queues. URL and content fingerprints prevent repeated work. Indexing is a downstream pipeline. Use leases for crash recovery, exponential backoff for failures, and metrics for frontier age, host errors, and duplicate rates.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Fetch through workers with per-host rate limits and robots policy checks. Normalize URLs, fingerprint content, and schedule recrawls by change likelihood.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Discuss retries, traps, malicious content, and pipeline observability. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify document size, concurrent editors, offline behavior, and conflict expectations. Choose an operation transformation or CRDT approach and define its tradeoffs.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: Clients submit edits with stable operation IDs and causal/version context to a document collaboration service. A room coordinator orders or merges operations using the chosen OT/CRDT model and broadcasts accepted updates. Durable operation logs support replay; periodic snapshots bound recovery time. Clients reconnect with a cursor and request missing operations. Presence is ephemeral and separate from durable content. Enforce document ACLs at join and operation time, and rate-limit abusive clients.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Persist an ordered operation log and periodically compact snapshots. Broadcast updates over persistent connections and authorize document membership.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Handle reconnect cursors, duplicate operations, presence, and version history. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify cacheable data, consistency, eviction, TTL, and acceptable stale reads. Choose key partitioning and replication strategy.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: Clients reach a cache proxy that maps keys to shards using a consistent hash ring. Each shard keeps data in memory with TTL and an eviction policy; replication depends on durability and latency needs. On misses, a bounded origin loader applies request coalescing and circuit breakers to avoid stampedes. Versioned keys or explicit invalidation handle updates. During shard loss, rebalance gradually and protect the source database with quotas and fallback caching.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Define get/set/invalidate behavior and protect against cache stampedes. Plan memory eviction, hot-key mitigation, and rolling resharding.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Discuss cache outage fallback, overload protection, and hit-rate observability. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Clarify inventory guarantees, queue fairness, payment timing, and cancellation policy. Separate browsing and search from authoritative inventory reservation.

sections.title: Core architecture
sections.body: Search and event pages are served from caches, but checkout goes through a queue that admits a controlled number of buyers. An inventory service performs atomic seat holds with short expirations and unique reservation IDs. Payment is handled asynchronously through an idempotent workflow; confirmed payment converts the hold into a ticket, while timeout or failure releases it. A reconciliation process handles late payment callbacks. Maintain a single authoritative seat state and measure queue wait, hold expiry, oversell attempts, and payment outcomes.

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Use a virtual waiting room to control admission and shed overload. Reserve inventory with atomic holds and expiry before payment confirmation.

sections.title: Reliability and operations
sections.body: Discuss idempotency, fraud, retries, and reconciliation of payment and inventory. Call out the main latency, availability, correctness, and cost tradeoffs; instrument the system and plan gradual capacity changes.

trend.title: From copilots to agentic workflows
trend.intro: Production agent engineering centers on measuring outcomes, tracing the full run, and keeping permissions and escalation paths clear.

points.title: Measure outcomes
points.text: Build task-specific evaluations into the development loop.

points.title: Observe the whole run
points.text: Trace tool calls, latency, cost, and handoffs.

points.title: Keep control legible
points.text: Bound permissions and define human escalation paths.

trend.readingSummary: Agent reliability is becoming an engineering discipline: evaluation, observability, and deliberate context design show up alongside model choice.
